patient.title: Carboplatin and paclitaxel · lung cancer
patient.purpose: After surgery, treatment aims to reduce the chance of lung cancer returning. For advanced lung cancer, it aims to control cancer and help symptoms. Your team confirms which aim applies to you.

agents.name: Paclitaxel
agents.explanation: Paclitaxel stabilises microtubules, structures cells use during division. It can slow cancer growth but also harm healthy nerves, blood-forming cells and hair follicles. Both medicines are planned on Day 1 of each of four cycles.
agents.watch: Tell the nurse immediately about infusion symptoms. Report numbness, tingling, fever, painful muscles, mouth sores or diarrhoea.

agents.name: Carboplatin
agents.explanation: Carboplatin forms links in DNA that hinder copying and repair. Healthy tissues can also be harmed. Its dose depends on target exposure (AUC) and measured or estimated kidney function; AUC is not a fixed number of milligrams. Both medicines are planned on Day 1 of each of four cycles.
agents.watch: Report fever, bleeding, nausea, hearing changes or numbness. Tell the nurse immediately about possible allergy during the infusion.

steps.title: Before the first visit
steps.text: Blood tests, relevant cardiac assessment, medicines review, fertility discussion and the consent conversation come first.

steps.title: Plan venous access
steps.text: A cannula, PICC or implanted port may be used. If a port is chosen, a trained team inserts it in a separate procedure with local anaesthetic and sometimes sedation; the team explains fasting, blood-thinner and wound instructions.

steps.title: Infusion day
steps.text: Staff check the line, give prescribed premedicines and treatment, and observe for reactions. Tell them immediately about burning, pain, rash or breathlessness.

steps.title: Home and next review
steps.text: This regimen does not routinely need a take-home infusion pump. Staff disconnect the infusion; a port is de-accessed when appropriate. Keep line-care and next-visit instructions.

details.title: Port insertion and removal
details.text: The line team explains placement, dressing care and when normal activities can resume. A port is accessed with a special needle during treatment. Removal of the implanted device is a separate planned procedure when no longer needed; do not remove or adjust it yourself.

details.title: PICC care and urgent line symptoms
details.text: A PICC usually needs regular dressing and flushing appointments even between treatments. Fever, redness, swelling, pain, leakage or damage requires prompt advice. Your hospital supplies the exact care instructions.

details.title: Visit time and transport
details.text: First visits can take longer because of loading doses, premedicines and observation. Ask the unit about expected time, transport and any escort needed after sedation or line insertion.

details.title: Phase-specific visit pattern

questions.q: What benefit is realistic for me and what other options are available?
questions.a: Treatment aims to control small-cell lung cancer after previous therapy and may help symptoms. The evidence is limited, so discuss likely benefit, burdens and alternatives with the team. A small uncontrolled study found some tumour responses to weekly paclitaxel in previously treated SCLC. The study used six weekly doses followed by two weeks without treatment, which differs from this NCCP schedule. It cannot establish a survival advantage over other treatment or supportive care.

questions.q: What are my confirmed infusion days, dose and planned review points?
questions.a: Paclitaxel is given on Days 1, 8 and 15 of each 28-day cycle. Day 22 is a planned week off, not a fourth infusion. Treatment continues while helping and tolerated; there is no fixed cycle limit.

questions.q: Who arranges and reviews my blood tests and scans?
questions.a: Blood count, kidney and liver tests at baseline and before each treatment. Review symptoms, function, neuropathy and infusion reactions before every dose. Scans follow the consultant’s individual plan. Ask who arranges and reviews the results.

questions.q: What premedication and anti-sickness plan should I follow?
questions.a: Follow the written plan for your exact prescription. Report missed premedication before infusion; confirm prevention and rescue medicines with the pharmacist.

questions.q: Which symptoms need an immediate call, and which number should I use?
questions.a: Call the oncology contact number immediately for fever, shivers or sudden illness, severe or new breathing difficulty, chest pain, fainting, severe abdominal pain or persistent diarrhoea. Tell staff immediately about infusion symptoms. Report new numbness, weakness, painful skin changes, swelling or visual changes promptly; do not wait for the next cycle. Keep the unit’s daytime and out-of-hours numbers on your treatment card.

evidence.title: Why this treatment may be chosen
evidence.intro: A small uncontrolled study found some tumour responses to weekly paclitaxel in previously treated SCLC. The study used six weekly doses followed by two weeks without treatment, which differs from this NCCP schedule. It cannot establish a survival advantage over other treatment or supportive care.
evidence.population: NCCP 00621 d: small-cell lung cancer that has returned or has not responded to previous treatment. This use is outside the Irish licence and requires the hospital off-label approval and consent process. This guide is for conventional paclitaxel alone.
evidence.interpretation: Discuss possible benefit, alternatives and uncertainty for your own situation. The treatment aim is cancer control and symptom relief.
evidence.limitations: Yamamoto 2006 enrolled 22 patients, with 21 eligible; it was a small single-arm phase II study without a control group. The trial schedule was 80 mg/m² weekly for six weeks of an eight-week cycle, not the NCCP Day 1/8/15 28-day schedule. Five partial responses were observed: three of 11 sensitive and two of 10 refractory cases. These counts are not a comparative efficacy estimate. The study cannot establish a survival benefit, modern treatment ranking or the expected response probability for the current NCCP schedule. NCCP explicitly flags 00621 d as off-label; publication and NCCP listing do not create an Irish product licence.

clinical.component_rationale: Cells use tiny structures called microtubules to separate their chromosomes when dividing. Paclitaxel stabilises these structures so they cannot rearrange normally, interrupting cell division. It can also affect nerves and other healthy tissues.

important_cautions: Yamamoto 2006 enrolled 22 patients, with 21 eligible; it was a small single-arm phase II study without a control group.
The trial schedule was 80 mg/m² weekly for six weeks of an eight-week cycle, not the NCCP Day 1/8/15 28-day schedule.
Five partial responses were observed: three of 11 sensitive and two of 10 refractory cases. These counts are not a comparative efficacy estimate.
The study cannot establish a survival benefit, modern treatment ranking or the expected response probability for the current NCCP schedule.
NCCP explicitly flags 00621 d as off-label; publication and NCCP listing do not create an Irish product licence.

support_summary: NCCP first-dose suggested premedication: dexamethasone 8 mg IV, chlorphenamine 10 mg IV and famotidine 20 mg IV 30 minutes before infusion.

From Day 8, NCCP permits omission of routine dexamethasone; previous reaction or higher risk requires consultant-directed adjustment. Famotidine omission is also a consultant/local-policy decision with close observation.
The actual conventional product SmPC uses a different generic premedication schedule. Reconcile the exact product and local protocol; no automatic patient-led omission or switch to nab-paclitaxel.
Consider analgesia for muscle/joint aches; review neuropathy before every dose and growth-factor support when indicated.
Low emetic risk: prevention and rescue medicines remain separate from reaction premedication. Confirm individual suitability, interactions and duration; this reference is not a prescription.

rationale.summary: A small uncontrolled study found some tumour responses to weekly paclitaxel in previously treated SCLC. The study used six weekly doses followed by two weeks without treatment, which differs from this NCCP schedule. It cannot establish a survival advantage over other treatment or supportive care.
